newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Physical cocoa demand still patchy in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Physical cocoa demand still patchy in Europe.

text.p: Cocoa continued to meet patchy demand for beans and products in Europe, with the limited offtake pushing up butter ratios but many in the industry remain sidelined by the unclear market outlook, physical traders said.
"We have seen some good demand for (cocoa) liquor and butter -- chocolate manufacturers have reported healthy sales and they're upping their production," one trader said.
Another cited market rumours that a German presser was having difficulties meeting its delivery commitments and this had caused extra demand for Dutch factories.
This offtake had firmed up butter ratios to above 2.80, with some quoting 2.85. Physical bean differentials were steady.
German cocoa traders said they had also noted some near-term buying of beans, butter and liquor (mass) which they attributed to a bunching of seasonal orders at one leading processor.

They quoted bean prices at 2.20 marks/kg for 1996 and 2.24 marks, down 0.04-0.10 marks on the week. The 1996 butter ratio had been boosted by three points to 2.83 after the recent spot purchases but the 1997 ratio was just 2.69, they added.

Others here described the upturn in demand as short-lived, dying away this week as the futures market picked itself up from six-month lows. The benchmark December contract fell to a low at 955 stg a tonne before recovering to trade around 20 stg higher on Thursday.
"Business is still very fragile and it dried up again as soon as the market moved higher," one trader said.
German industry had also not abandoned its reluctant buying strategy and orders for 1997 were not forthcoming due to price premiums over nearby cocoa and a strong sterling/mark rate.
Dutch traders said the two imponderables hanging over the market were what would happen to the cocoa taken delivery of on September and the size and timing of next season's crops.

"The direction of the market is still very much up in the air and it's very difficult to make a decision to come into the market on that basis," one said. "We could still be looking at hardly any deficit at all or one of 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes."

Reports doing the rounds in the market were still pointing to higher crop levels than originally predicted. Traders had no fresh forecasts but agreed that for the Ivorian main crop, the total had climbed from 800,000 tonnes to above 900,000. Fears over serious delays to the crop had also diminished, they added.

Most other African origins looked to be in similar shape. Traders said the Cameroon crop appeared to be on time and a "good but not fantastic" size. Nigeria was also forecast on time and average to good in size. Only Ghana may be a little late and slightly below normal levels, they added.
"With the exception of Ghana, it all looks to be a little better," one commented.

But German traders said any further bearish Ivorian crop reports would boost the market and recalled last year's late delivery tactics at origin when European prices rose as bean volumes were diverted to U.S. consumers. --Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
